← Concrete lifting bid calculator

How much to charge for concrete lifting

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$4.50 per square foot” or “$75 per hole” special. That number is not a takeoff. An 80-square-foot sidewalk with a one-inch void and the truck parked at the curb is not the same job as a 400-square-foot driveway with a four-inch void, polyurethane, a backyard hose run, six extra holes, and joint seal. The trip is the same. The cubic feet are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the void and the extras, not just “square feet of slab”

Concrete-pour calculators price cubic yards of new mix. A lift is a different job: the method, the void volume, the access path, the extra holes, and the extras that are not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published per-square-foot special is how the first extra hole eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each inch of void is fill that never appears on the coupon. Extra holes, joint seal, and a backyard hose run are billed as their own hours. Polyurethane is an adder that gets forgotten on a mudjacking special. On the sample rates a 400-square-foot driveway with a four-inch void, poly, a backyard hose, six extra holes, and joint seal prices about $13,562.80 (19.2 crew-hours, $33.91 / sf). The same shop’s 80-square-foot sidewalk hang prices about $897.77 (4.0 hours, walk-away $628.44, $11.22 / sf).

Matching the $4.50 / sf special already loses about $268 on the sidewalk hang ($360 against a $628 walk-away), and it loses about $7,694 on the poly backyard whose walk-away is already $9,493.96.

A two-inch mud driveway is not automatically a markup on the sidewalk

A 280-square-foot driveway with a two-inch void, mudjacking, street-side access, and joint seal is not the sidewalk special plus 15%. On the sample rates that driveway prices about $2,455.74 (12.3 crew-hours). An occupied 200-square-foot warehouse floor with a two-inch void, poly, four extra holes, and containment prices about $5,278.29 (12.9 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first extra hole.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h operator loaded at 32% payroll burden is $55.44. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number. Zero void depth still prices: pump hours are the void, not an error.

What this is not

This is not a structural design, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. The slab area, the void depth, the method, access, extra holes, and joint seal are yours to confirm. It does not price a new concrete pour, a basement waterproofing job, or an epoxy garage floor.

Price your concrete lift

Common questions

How much to charge for concrete lifting?

Charge from the trip, the lift setup, the void cubic feet (area times depth over 12), the method (mud or poly), the access path, extra holes, joint seal, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 80-square-foot sidewalk with a one-inch void, mudjacking, and street-side access, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $898 (4.0 crew-hours, $11.22 per square foot).

Why is a $4.50 per square foot lifting special dangerous?

Homeowners count square feet of slab. Void volume, polyurethane versus slurry, backyard hose runs, extra holes, and occupied-building containment do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a sidewalk is how a four-inch poly backyard job becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $4.50 special ($360 on 80 sf) already loses about $268 against the $628 walk-away on the sidewalk hang, and it loses about $7,694 on the 400 sf poly backyard whose walk-away is already $9,494.

How much to charge for polyjacking a driveway with a deep void?

A 400-square-foot driveway with a four-inch void, polyurethane, a backyard hose run, six extra holes, and joint seal is not an 80-square-foot sidewalk. On the sample rates that job prices around $13,563 (19.2 crew-hours, $33.91 per square foot), while a sidewalk special hang prices around $898 (4.0 hours). The same shop's 280-square-foot two-inch mud driveway with joint seal prices around $2,456 (12.3 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Bid the void, the method, and the access.

Price a mudjacking or polyjacking job the way the trade actually loses money: void cubic feet, backyard hose runs, extra holes, joint seal, and occupied-building containment as their own hours. You get the bid, the hours the first four-inch poly backyard hang actually consumes, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The slab

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard or a structural design — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise “$4.50 a square foot” for slab lifting?

      Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: an 80 sq ft sidewalk with a 1-inch void, mudjacked, truck parked street-side. It really does price low. What the per-square-foot number cannot see is method, void depth, access, extra holes, and joint sealing. Price your actual slab beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items you can show the homeowner instead of an argument about who is honest.

      Why does polyurethane cost so much more in material than mudjacking, when it’s faster?

      They trade material cost for labor and cure time. Mudjacking starts at $7.50 of slurry per cubic foot of void and 0.18 crew-hours per cubic foot. Polyurethane foam starts at $48 per cubic foot — more than six times the material — but only 0.09 crew-hours per cubic foot, roughly half the labor, and it sets in minutes instead of days. Neither number is universally cheaper; the void volume and how fast the customer needs the slab back decide which one wins on a given job.

      Why does backyard or interior access add hours if the void volume is the same?

      Because moving the pump and hose is not part of drilling the hole. A driveway job with the truck parked at the slab adds no access hours. A backyard job run through a hose or a gate adds 1.6 hours for the extra distance. An occupied interior floor adds 2.8 hours for containment, protection, and working around furniture and foot traffic. All three can lift the exact same void volume at very different total prices.

      Is this the same as pouring a new slab, or basement waterproofing?

      No. This prices lifting an existing settled slab back toward level with mudjacking or polyurethane — it is not a new-slab pour (that is cubic yards of fresh concrete) and not basement waterproofing (a French drain, a sump pit, and a discharge line). If the slab is cracked beyond repair or the settling is a foundation problem rather than a void under a walk or drive, lifting is the wrong tool and this calculator will still happily price the wrong job.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your slab size, wages, or prices. Only your business details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser’s local storage so you do not retype them, and the customer’s details are never saved.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — pump hours, access time, slurry or foam, extra holes, and joint sealing — the point below which the lift stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-rate-special.html.text:
← Concrete Lifting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat “$X/sq ft” or “$X/hole” special

Shops get quoted a published $4.50/sq ft or $75/hole special. That rate cannot see the void — an 80 sq ft sidewalk with a one-inch void and the truck at the curb is not the same job as a 400 sq ft backyard driveway with a four-inch void, polyurethane, a hose run, six extra holes, and joint seal.

What a flat rate special is

A per-square-foot or per-hole special is the fastest number to publish or quote over the phone: multiply the footprint, or count the holes, and read back a total. It is what a homeowner finds on a postcard or a competitor's website and asks you to match.

The rate behind it was set from one job — a given void depth, a given method, a given access path, no extra holes, no sealing — and then reused for the next slab that calls, whether or not that slab shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the slab area, the void depth, the method — mudjacking or polyurethane — the access path — street-side, backyard, or interior — extra holes past the included set, and whether joint seal is included, plus your own hourly wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment cost, overhead, and target margin. It turns the void into cubic feet the way pump time and fill material actually scale, prices method and access as their own hours, and returns the price, the price per square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this lift, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a one-inch settle and a four-inch settle on a similar footprint, even though the deeper void needs 20 times the fill volume on this page's own worked examples. Computes void cubic feet as slab square feet × void depth ÷ 12 for every job, so a deeper void orders more pump hours and material without anyone eyeballing a markup.
Has no separate line for method — a mudjacked sidewalk and a polyjacked driveway of the same size get the same rate, even though polyurethane foam runs far more per cubic foot than slurry. Starts pump hours and material cost per cubic foot from a mudjacking or polyurethane preset, editable to the shop's own suppliers.
Has no line for access — a truck-at-the-curb job and a backyard hose-and-pump run, or an occupied interior floor, get the same rate. Prices street-side, backyard, or interior access as its own hours line, separate from the void.
Prices extra holes and joint seal, if at all, as part of the blended rate, so a job that needs six extra holes and a full seal costs the same as one that needs neither. Prices extra holes and joint seal / crack fill as their own hours and material lines, added only when the job needs them.
Gives the customer a number to compare against a competitor's coupon, not a number to check a quote against. Reports price per square foot, effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price alongside the bid price, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

A sidewalk special applied to a backyard hang

Using this calculator's own shipped starting inputs — $42 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, $95 travel and equipment, 16% overhead, 30% target margin, $175 mobilization, and the method's own starting pump and material rates:

JobVoidWalk-away priceBid price (30% margin)
80 sq ft sidewalk, 1″ void, mudjacked, street-side (this calculator's own shipped default)6.67 cu ft$628.44$897.77
400 sq ft backyard driveway, 4″ void, polyjacked, 6 extra holes, joint seal133.33 cu ft$9,493.96$13,562.80

The sidewalk prices at $11.22 per square foot. Apply that same learned rate to the backyard driveway's 400 square feet and the quote comes to $4,488.87 — $5,005.09 below the driveway's own walk-away cost of $9,493.96, before counting the $9,073.93 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 30% target margin. Same idea, one flat rate, one job it happens to price near and one job it loses money on the moment the void, the method, and the extras change.

Worked from calc.mjs's own calculateBid against the tool's shipped default job (mudjacking, street-side, 80 sq ft, 1-inch void, no extras) and its own “backyard, polyurethane, extras” preset (400 sq ft, 4-inch void, 6 extra holes, joint seal) — not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check either row yourself.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate special get a lifting job wrong?

Because a lift is priced by the void it fills, not by the slab's square footage or its hole count alone. Void cubic feet equal slab square feet times void depth in inches, divided by 12. An 80-square-foot sidewalk settled one inch has about 6.67 cubic feet of void. A 400-square-foot driveway settled four inches has about 133.33 cubic feet -- 20 times as much fill for five times the square footage. A rate learned from the sidewalk and reused on the driveway prices the void as if it barely changed, because square footage and hole count cannot tell a one-inch settle from a four-inch one.

What else does a flat special leave out?

Method, access, and the extras past the coupon. Polyurethane foam costs several times as much per cubic foot as mudjacking slurry, but sets faster and needs less pump time. A backyard hose-and-pump run or an occupied interior floor adds its own access hours that a street-side truck job never has. Extra holes past the included set and joint seal or crack fill after lifting are their own labor and material lines, not something a flat per-square-foot or per-hole number has anywhere to put.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting inputs -- a $42 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, 16% overhead, and a 30% target margin: an 80 square foot sidewalk with a 1-inch void, mudjacked, truck at the curb, walks away at $628.44 and prices at $897.77 -- $11.22 per square foot. A 400 square foot backyard driveway with a 4-inch void, polyjacked, six extra holes, and joint seal walks away at $9,493.96 and prices at $13,562.80. Quoting the driveway at the sidewalk's learned rate of $11.22 per square foot comes to $4,488.87 -- $5,005.09 below the driveway's own walk-away cost, and $9,073.93 short of what this calculator says the job should charge at a 30% target margin.

Is a flat special ever a reasonable way to quote a lift?

For a job close to the one the special was set on -- a small slab, a shallow void, street-side access, no extra holes, no sealing -- a flat rate can land close, and this calculator's own sidewalk example prices near typical special rates. The risk is applying that same rate to a deeper void, foam instead of slurry, backyard or interior access, or extra holes and joint seal stacked on top, because a flat per-square-foot or per-hole number has no way to see any of those until the crew is already on site.

Does this calculator know my local material or labor rates?

No. It has no data on your local slurry or foam supplier's price or your crew's wage. It takes the slab area, void depth, method, access path, extra holes, and joint seal you enter, plus your own hourly wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into void cubic feet, crew hours, and a price for this lift -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

← Concrete Lifting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. QuoteIQ

Two different shapes: QuoteIQ is a paid, ongoing field-service app for running a concrete-leveling business's whole quoting, scheduling, and job-costing pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one mudjacking or polyjacking job cost, given its void volume, method, and access, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

QuoteIQ is a field-service business app marketed at concrete-leveling and general contracting crews, covering on-site quote building (with a built-in measurement tool), scheduling, job costing against the quote once work starts, invoicing, and customer follow-up across a whole business. It is a paid, account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across every job you run, not a one-off calculator. QuoteIQ's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a subscription field-service app aimed in part at concrete-leveling contractors — is stated, and no dollar amount for QuoteIQ appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what QuoteIQ does. It does not build a quote from a phone-camera measurement, schedule a crew, or track job costs after the fact, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one lift's slab area and void depth, method — mudjacking or polyurethane — access path — street-side, backyard, or interior — extra holes, joint seal, and occupied- building containment, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or QuoteIQ?

They fit different points in the job. QuoteIQ is a paid, ongoing field-service app aimed at concrete-leveling and general contracting businesses, covering on-site quote building, scheduling, job costing, and customer follow-up across every job a crew runs, sold as a subscription. A concrete-leveling shop that already runs its whole quoting, scheduling, and job-costing pipeline through one app is better served by QuoteIQ or a comparable platform; a crew that wants an instant, private answer to what one lift should cost from its void volume, method, and access before opening a business system is in the right place here.
